Exam question [3]

Explain what happens in the muscles when you exercise at a high intensity.
3 marks
Mark scheme — individual marking pointsAny 3 of 5 = full marks [3]
✓Heart and lungs cannot supply enough oxygen to the muscles fast enough[1]
✓Less aerobic respiration occurs (so less ATP / energy is released)[1]
✓Muscles switch to anaerobic respiration (glucose → lactic acid)[1]
✓Lactic acid builds up in the muscle cells[1]
✓Causes muscle fatigue / cramp (and creates an oxygen debt)[1]
Command word: EXPLAIN
Link each step with so / because — aim for 3+ distinct scientific points.
slides.newHtml:
Exam question [3]

Explain what happens in the muscles when you exercise at a high intensity.
3 marks
Mark scheme — linked chain (EXPLAIN)Any 3 linked points (max 3)
1Heart & lungs cannot supply enough oxygen to muscles fast enough[1]
↓so…
2Less aerobic respiration occurs (and less ATP / energy is released)[1]
↓therefore…
3Muscles switch to anaerobic respiration (glucose → lactic acid)[1]
↓which causes…
4Lactic acid builds up in muscle cells[1]
↓leading to…

slides.title: Weight: example & your turn
slides.newHtml:
Weight: example & your turn

Worked example (FIFA)
An astronaut has mass 80 kg on Mars (g = 3.8 N/kg). Calculate her weight.
F: W = m × g
I: W = 80 × 3.8
A: W = 304 N
Your turn (whiteboards)
1. Same astronaut on Jupiter (g = 26 N/kg).
→ W = 80 × 26 = 2080 N
2. A rover weighs 760 N on Mars (g = 3.8 N/kg). Find its mass.
→ m = W ÷ g = 760 ÷ 3.8 = 200 kg
3. What is the rover’s mass on Earth?
→ Still 200 kg (mass never changes!)

slides.title: Mass vs weight on the Moon

When the astronaut lands on the Moon, what happens to their mass and weight?
ABoth mass and weight decrease
BMass stays 70 kg; weight drops from 700 N to 112 N
CWeight stays 700 N; mass drops to 11.2 kg
⚠ EXAMINER TIP: Mass (kg) is constant everywhere — only WEIGHT (N) changes with g!

slides.title: Orbital speed
slides.newHtml:
Orbital speed

v=2πrT
  • r = orbital radius (distance from centre)
  • T = time period (time for one full orbit)
  • Closer bodies feel stronger gravity → move faster

slides.title: Orbital speed: watch the units
slides.newHtml:
Orbital speed: watch the units

orbital speed=2 × π × orbital radiustime period
SI units → m/s
r in m, T in s
Distance
km → m: × 1000
Time
h → s: × 3600  |  d → s: × 86 400

slides.title: Worked example: Mercury
slides.newHtml:
Worked example: Mercury

QUESTION: Mercury orbits the Sun in 87.97 days with orbital radius 57.91 million km. Calculate its orbital speed in m/s (3 s.f.).
F — Formula & convert to SI units first
v = 2πr ÷ T  |  r = 5.791 × 1010 m  |  T = 87.97 × 86 400 = 7 600 608 s
I — Insert values into the formula
v = (2 × π × 5.791 × 1010) ÷ 7 600 608
F / A — Fine-tune & Answer with units
v = 47 900 m/s (or 4.14 million km/day)

A geostationary satellite orbits once every 24 hours at height 35 000 km above Earth’s surface (Earth’s radius = 6400 km). Find its speed in m/s.

slides.title: How stars are born
slides.newHtml:
How stars are born

1. Nebula
Giant cloud of hydrogen gas and dust pulled together by gravity over millions of years
2. Protostar
Collapsing core becomes hot and dense (gravitational potential → thermal energy)
3. Main sequence star
Hot enough in the core → hydrogen fusion ignites: a star is born!

slides.title: Main sequence stars
slides.newHtml:
Main sequence stars

For most of a star’s life, it is stable:
Inward force
Gravity pulls all the gas inwards
Outward force
Heat & radiation pressure from hydrogen fusion push outwards
Inward gravity = Outward pressure → STABLE

slides.title: Leaving the main sequence
slides.newHtml:
Leaving the main sequence

Why does a star like the Sun leave the main sequence?
AGravity stops pulling inwards, so the star drifts apart
BCore hydrogen runs out → forces become unbalanced → outer layers expand & cool into a red giant
CThe star instantly explodes in a supernova
⚠ EXAM KEY: Main sequence = balanced forces. Core hydrogen running out breaks that balance!

slides.title: Red giants
slides.newHtml:
Red giants

When core hydrogen runs out, the star leaves the main sequence:
  • The outer layers expand enormously
  • Its surface becomes much cooler
  • Cooler surface → glows red
Later it sheds its outer layers, leaving a tiny, hot white dwarf

Supernova

A red supergiant collapses violently and explodes
  • Can outshine an entire galaxy for weeks
  • About one every 50 years in a galaxy like the Milky Way
  • Leaves behind a neutron star or a black hole

Black holes

Formed by the collapse of the most massive stars
  • All the star’s remaining mass is crushed into a tiny point
  • Gravitational field strength is unimaginably strong
Past the event horizon, not even light can escape!

slides.title: Your turn: fill the gaps
slides.newHtml:
Your turn: fill the gaps

The gas and dust in a nebula is pulled together by gravity. It heats up and becomes a protostar. When it is hot enough, fusion starts. Gravity is balanced by pressure: it is now a main sequence star.

slides.title: Exam question: massive stars
slides.newHtml:
Exam question: massive stars

Describe the evolution of a star with a mass much larger than the Sun, starting from a nebula.[4]
1. A nebula (gas & dust) collapses under gravity → heats up to form a protostar
↓ 2. Core heats enough for hydrogen fusion → massive main sequence star (balanced forces)
↓ 3. Core hydrogen runs out → expands and cools into a red supergiant
↓ 4. Core collapses violently and explodes as a supernova
↓ 5. Leaves a dense neutron star or (if massive enough) a black hole
Mark scheme: Any 4 linked points in logical order (max 4 marks)
Check your wording
Say red supergiant — not just red giant — for massive stars!
